title: Liquid Penetrant Testing for Refineries | Dye PT (US)
description: Dye penetrant inspection for US refinery stainless piping, alloy overlay and weld repairs, with controlled chemistry for alloys. Request a PT quote today.
h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing for Refineries: Stainless, Alloy Overlay and Repair Welds
html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes Level II technicians to US refineries for liquid penetrant testing, also called dye penetrant inspection, on stainless steel, nickel alloy, alloy overlay and other non-magnetic components where magnetic particle methods do not work. Penetrant shows cracks that are open to the surface: stress corrosion cracking, fatigue and weld defects on piping, vessels, exchangers and valves. Request a PT inspection quote with your weld or component list.

Where penetrant fits in a refinery

Penetrant is the method of choice when the metal is not ferromagnetic or when the part has awkward geometry that a magnetic field cannot cover. In a refinery that means the austenitic stainless piping and vessel internals in hydroprocessing and hydrogen units, nickel-alloy weld overlay on reactor and column parts, aluminum and copper-alloy items, and small fittings with socket and threaded welds. It also works on carbon steel when the owner prefers it, though magnetic particle is usually faster there; see magnetic particle inspection for refineries.

Penetrant sees only flaws open to the surface. It will not tell you whether a crack runs deeper than the surface trace or whether a weld has lack of fusion below the surface; ultrasonic testing, described on the UT for refineries page, covers that side.

Cracking and damage penetrant is asked to find

  • Polythionic acid stress corrosion cracking. Sensitized stainless steel in hydroprocessing and reformer units can crack during shutdown when sulfur compounds, moisture and air form acid. After a turnaround, inspectors often ask for penetrant on the welds and heat-affected zones of exposed stainless piping and reactor internals.
  • Chloride stress corrosion cracking. Stainless steel under wet insulation or in contact with chloride-bearing deposits develops branched surface cracks. Penetrant is the usual way to confirm them once the insulation is stripped.
  • Thermal and mechanical fatigue. Mix points, quench zones and vibrating small-bore stainless connections crack at weld toes.
  • Overlay and cladding defects. Alloy overlay on carbon steel vessels is examined by penetrant after welding and after any repair, looking for cracks and porosity open to the surface.
  • Fabrication defects on repairs. Root and final passes on piping repairs, seat areas on valves and weld buildup on pump parts.

API 571 describes these mechanisms, API 510 and 570 steer when the owner's inspector requests examination, and the scope on any job is whatever that inspector marks on the drawing.

Technique: how a field penetrant test is actually done

  1. Clean. Remove oil, paint, scale and weld flux. Contaminants plug the surface openings the penetrant needs to enter, so poor cleaning causes false clean results.
  2. Apply penetrant. The usual refinery choice is a visible red-dye, solvent-removable penetrant in aerosol cans, applied by spray or brush over the whole area plus a margin.
  3. Dwell. The penetrant sits for the time stated in the procedure, which depends on material, flaw type and temperature. Dwell times are not shortened to catch up on a schedule.
  4. Remove excess. Surface penetrant is wiped away with clean, lint-free cloth lightly moistened with solvent, never sprayed directly, which would wash flaws clean.
  5. Develop. A thin, even coat of white developer draws penetrant out of flaws and produces a visible bleed-out.
  6. Examine. The technician looks within the time window in the procedure, under the minimum light level ASME Section V Article 6 requires, and records every relevant indication.
  7. Clean up. Residue is removed; stainless parts, in particular, should not be left with developer on them.

Temperature matters. Standard procedures apply within a stated range of surface temperature; outside it, the technique must be demonstrated on a test block at that temperature before use. In a refinery, a pipe in the sun in July or a cold line in January can fall outside the range, so tell us the metal temperature.

Material controls that protect stainless and nickel alloys

Penetrant materials for austenitic stainless steel and nickel-based alloys must be low in chlorine, fluorine and sulfur. ASTM E165 and ASME Section V Article 6 set the controls, and the procedure requires us to use certified batches and record the lot numbers on the report. This is not a formality. Residual halogens left on hot stainless can contribute to the very cracking we are looking for. If your site has its own material restrictions, send them with the request so the procedure matches.

For more on stainless components, see penetrant testing of stainless steel, and for weld-specific scopes, penetrant testing of welds.

Visible dye or fluorescent penetrant

Most refinery penetrant work uses visible red dye because it needs no darkened area and works in daylight with a white-light meter. Fluorescent penetrant is more sensitive and can find finer cracks, but it requires an ultraviolet lamp and a dark enclosure, which is hard on a scaffold beside a column. We choose fluorescent only when the owner's specification asks for it, for example on critical rotating equipment parts in a shop setting, and tell you up front so the crew carries the right kit. A given component must be examined with one family of penetrant; switching from visible to fluorescent after the part has been contaminated with dye is not permitted without cleaning to the procedure.

Valves, small-bore connections and shop-type parts

A turnaround always produces a pile of small items that need surface examination: valve seat and body repairs, pump casing weld repairs, small-bore branch connections replaced during the outage and spool pieces made in a fab shop. Penetrant is practical for these because there is no need for a magnetic field and no need for access on two sides. Socket welds are a special case. A socket weld has a small gap that traps cleaner and penetrant, so extra care in cleaning and removal is needed to separate a true crack from a bleed-out of trapped material. We note any pattern that could be trapped liquid rather than a flaw, and we re-clean and re-test before calling it.

Weld overlay and cladding

Many vessels in hydroprocessing and sour service carry a stainless or nickel-alloy overlay on the inside surface to resist corrosion. The overlay is deposited by welding and then examined for cracks and porosity open to the surface. After any repair to the overlay, the same examination is repeated on the repaired area. An overlay crack matters because it can let process fluid reach the carbon steel behind it, so inspectors look at overlay carefully during major outages. Penetrant gives them a fast, visual answer without heavy equipment. Interpretation of an overlay indication, including whether it can stay in service, belongs to the owner's engineer.

Penetrant versus the alternatives in a refinery

Choosing a surface method on refinery parts
PartBest surface methodWhy
Austenitic stainless piping weldsPenetrantNot magnetic
Alloy overlay on a vessel shellPenetrantOverlay is non-magnetic and surface flaws are the target
Carbon steel nozzle weldsMagnetic particle, penetrant if preferredMT is faster and detects shallow subsurface flaws
Small-bore socket weldsPenetrant or MT, by materialGeometry limits yoke access
Corroded piping thicknessNeitherUse UT

The decision logic is laid out in our MT versus PT guide, and the Article 6 explainer walks through the code rules.

Planning for refinery work

Penetrant is a solvent job, and solvent-based cleaners and penetrants are flammable. Sites decide where aerosol cans can be used, what ventilation and permits are needed, and how wipes are disposed of. Many turnaround schedules place penetrant after weld repair and cleaning, so share the sequence to avoid an arrival at an unprepared surface. Technicians travel to your site and are mobilized for the agreed scope; expect site orientation, permits, gas monitoring and, near ports, TWIC. Confined-space entry for vessel internals follows the owner's permit system. If coatings or lagging must be removed first, the owner's crew does that before we start. Scaffold and rope access are set by the site. Our turnaround and shutdown page describes how a scope fits an outage.

Reporting: what you receive

  • Component, weld and line identification tied to the owner's drawing.
  • Procedure number and revision, with the code section governing examination and acceptance.
  • Penetrant, cleaner and developer product names with certified batch numbers and halogen or sulfur certificates for alloy work.
  • Surface preparation, metal temperature, dwell time and light level.
  • The Level II technician who performed the work, plus the name of the ASNT Level III who approved the method and reviewed the finished report.
  • Indications with location, size and orientation, a sketch or photo, and accept or reject against the cited criteria.

Acceptance normally follows the construction or repair code, such as ASME B31.3 for piping or Section VIII for vessels. The owner's inspector decides what to do with a rejectable flaw. Atlantis does not set remaining life or intervals.

What to send us for a quote

  • Drawings or a weld list with equipment and line numbers.
  • Base material and any overlay; stainless and nickel alloy grades matter.
  • Quantity, component size and surface finish.
  • Governing code or owner specification, and any restrictions on penetrant chemistry.
  • Metal temperature range, coatings or insulation, and access method.
  • Site address, safety orientation, permits and your outage dates.

Where we work in the US for refining

  • Houston: hydroprocessing and hydrogen units along the Ship Channel.
  • Beaumont: Southeast Texas refineries with large stainless piping inventories.
  • Baton Rouge: river corridor refineries with both carbon and alloy systems.
  • Lake Charles: refinery and processing sites on the Calcasieu channel.
  • Corpus Christi: South Texas refining and marine terminals.
  • Los Angeles: California refineries and hydrogen plants.
  • Philadelphia: Delaware River refining and process plants.
  • Gary: steel and refining around the southern shore of Lake Michigan.

Training your own technicians

If you want in-house penetrant capability, start with PT Level 1 and PT Level 2 theory, and practice in the penetrant testing simulator. Your company certifies its own personnel under a written practice built on SNT-TC-1A; our written practice development service helps build one. The oil and gas NDT training page covers programs for refinery teams, and the national penetrant testing page gives an overview.

What we do not do

Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States and does not offer specialist techniques on this page. We do not decide fitness for service; that belongs to your inspector and engineer. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001.

faq.q: Is liquid penetrant testing suitable for stainless steel refinery piping?
faq.a: Yes, it is the usual surface method for austenitic stainless because the material is not magnetic. We use penetrant materials certified low in chlorine, fluorine and sulfur and record the batch numbers on the report.
Anything that is not open to the surface, such as a buried lack of fusion or internal corrosion. Wall loss and subsurface weld flaws need ultrasonic testing, sometimes in the same mobilization.

faq.q: What do you need to quote PT on a turnaround?
faq.a: A component or weld list, material grades, quantities, the governing code, metal temperature, coatings or insulation, access and your dates. Special chemistry limits on your site should be included too.

faq.q: Can penetrant be used on a hot line?
faq.a: Only within the temperature range in the procedure. Outside that range, the technique has to be demonstrated on a test block at the actual temperature, so give us the surface temperature before you schedule.

faq.q: Why is dwell time so important?
faq.a: The penetrant needs time to enter tight cracks. Cutting dwell short can leave real flaws unseen, which is why we hold the time in the procedure even when the schedule is tight.

faq.q: Who accepts or rejects penetrant indications?
faq.a: The owner's inspector accepts or rejects against the code criteria cited in the procedure, such as B31.3 or Section VIII. We report each indication and the criteria we measured it against.

faq.q: Do you remove coatings before PT?
faq.a: The owner's crew normally strips coatings and insulation. We can clean the examination surface with solvent, but penetrant cannot work through paint, scale or weld flux.

faq.q: Will penetrant residue damage stainless equipment?
faq.a: Controlled materials do not, but leftover developer and cleaner can trap contaminants. We remove residue after the examination, and the report records the cleanup step.

faq.q: Do you travel to refineries outside the Gulf Coast?
faq.a: Yes. Crews mobilize anywhere in the United States, including California, the Mid-Atlantic and the Midwest, and the lead time depends on the site's credential requirements.
